cards.title: Write 12 months of emails in one sitting
cards.summary: Block out a full year of emails in a single session so the perceived cost of starting an email program collapses.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to start or restart a store email program and dreading the ongoing workload.
steps: Commit to a small, finite batch first: 12 or 24 emails, not an open-ended commitment.
Sit down once and write them all in one block (Hormozi says 24 emails took him roughly half a day).
Realize from that session that a year of list communication costs about half a day, which reframes email as cheap rather than as another plate to spin.
Start with once a month if you have never mailed; treat anything beyond the pre-written batch as bonus.
Prefer a quality threshold over a rigid cadence if committing to a schedule makes your writing worse — send when you have good material, not to satisfy a calendar.
caveats: Source-specific: this is Hormozi's own framing of his hesitation; the half-day figure is his, not a benchmark.
Batching works for evergreen tactical content; it is poorly suited to inventory drops, launches or time-sensitive promotions.

cards.title: Plain-text email format to stay out of the Promotions tab
cards.summary: Format marketing emails to look like a personal note — text-heavy, no images, one or two links — so filters treat them as real correspondence.
cards.use_when: Planning the HTML/template for any store campaign email, especially retention and re-engagement sends.
steps: Write the email as mostly text with a handful of sentences, approximating an everyday email between two people.
Send zero images where possible; if you must, keep them minimal, since image-heavy 'Vegas Strip' promotional layouts read as pure promotion to filters.
Limit to one or two links maximum per email.
Remove money-related language from the body and subject where you can — Hormozi observed more money words correlate with a higher share landing in the Promotions tab.
Ask recipients to reply as part of the flow (see the Reply Yes card) because replies signal engagement to providers.
Mentally model the provider's objective: they want to deliver the highest-quality inbox experience, so align with that instead of hunting hacks.
caveats: The source notes 16.9% of B2B marketing emails never reach the inbox at all, driven by domain reputation — plain text is one input, not a silver bullet.
No images means you cannot show product photography, so this format suits tactical/editorial sends more than visual product launches.

cards.title: The Money Minute structure: reward on every step
cards.summary: Use a fixed four-part email skeleton that rewards the reader for opening, for reading, and for clicking.
cards.use_when: Designing the standard template for a recurring store newsletter or retention email.
steps: Open with an immediate one-glance reward — a quote, a striking line or a tweet — so the reader is paid back the instant they open.
Follow with one single tactical idea, kept to roughly 200 words (about a minute of reading); resist adding a second concept.
Frame the tactic as problem → solution → how: name a condition that makes the solution necessary, give the solution, then the concrete tactic.
Insert a contextual CTA that bridges from that specific content rather than a generic copy-pasted button.
Close with a P.S., because after the subject line it is the most-read part of an email.
Keep the format identical every send so readers know exactly what they are getting — the McDonalds principle: same shape, different quality burger each time.
caveats: Hormozi explicitly says the 200-word limit is his format choice, not a rule of law — his colleague Lila sends longer story-based emails to higher-revenue segments and they perform well.
Placement of CTA vs P.S. is flexible; the source says there is no science to it.

cards.title: Reward every step with a feedback-loop email design
cards.summary: Behavior repeats when it was rewarded last time, so design each email so opening, reading and clicking each deliver a payoff.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an underperforming store newsletter or welcome sequence where readers open but never act.
steps: Analyze behavior as after-the-fact reward, not as a preceding trigger: people repeat actions that previously paid off.
Reward the open with a one-glance payoff at the very top of the body (quote, punchline, striking stat).
Reward the read with a complete, usable tactic — the reader should be able to apply it to their business immediately.
Reward the click by placing high-value hidden content behind the link (a video, a deeper document) rather than duplicating the email content.
Protect the loop: one bad email can break the habit, so prefer extending a silence over sending something weak.
Accept that failing to earn opens and clicks eventually pushes the sender toward the Promotions tab — the source calls this 'email death'.
caveats: A single poor send can undo accumulated trust, so the model punishes volume without quality.
Rewards must be real; promising value behind a link and not delivering it is treated by the source as the worst outcome.

cards.title: Reply Yes onboarding to train provider reputation
cards.summary: Require new subscribers to reply 'Yes' to receive the lead magnet, so engagement signals raise sender reputation.
cards.use_when: Setting up or revising the welcome and lead-magnet delivery flow for a store's opt-in.
steps: Structure the welcome email so the lead magnet is delivered only after the subscriber replies 'Yes'.
Give a reason to reply by making the reward clearly worth the action (e.g. an exclusive chapter or asset).
Use the pre-reward moment to sell regular communication, not just the freebie — subscribers who only want the magnet will ignore everything after.
Place the lead magnet mention near the end, after you have sold the ongoing value, so you surprise and delight before giving the promised item.
Inside the gated asset, continue the loop by pointing to specific pages and asking for further engagement.
Treat this as building domain reputation with inbox providers — many small positive signals rather than one hack.
caveats: Reputation is cumulative; the source describes it as '100 golden BBs', not a single silver bullet.
Reply-gating adds friction, so it will reduce raw opt-in-to-magnet completion compared with instant delivery.

cards.title: Make unsubscribing easy to protect deliverability
cards.summary: Reduce friction on unsubscribes because dormant subscribers hurt domain reputation more than people who leave cleanly.
cards.use_when: Configuring the unsubscribe link, preference center and list hygiene for a store's email program.
steps: Make the unsubscribe action visible and simple rather than buried or requiring a support request.
Reason from deliverability: uninterested subscribers who stay on the list drag down domain-level sending reputation over time.
Treat a subscriber who unsubscribes as still aware of your brand — they may still buy later through another channel or inbox, so do not treat it as a loss.
Accept a higher unsubscribe rate on your first send in a long while — the source calls this 'shaking the tree', effectively pulling forward churn.
Benchmark against it: Hormozi reports over 1% on his first-ever send, settling to roughly 0.42% per email, and treats the program as healthy as long as list growth between sends exceeds unsubscribes.
caveats: The 1% / 0.42% figures are one sender's list, not a target for all stores.
If unsubscribes exceed growth, the reasoning inverts and the cadence or content is the problem.

cards.title: Segment the list by qualifier answers at opt-in
cards.summary: Collect qualifiers like revenue band or business stage at signup and send content matched to the segment.
cards.use_when: Designing the opt-in form and deciding who receives which store campaign or educational email.
steps: Add qualifying questions to the opt-in — for example revenue band, whether they run a business, or product-usage level for a store.
Route sends by segment (e.g. a specific tactic only to the 500k+ group, another to 0–100k).
Recognize that mismatch, not email quality, is usually why a send underperforms — advanced content to beginners or the reverse reads as 'not for me'.
Encourage honest answers: subscribers who lie to get the 'better' tier receive content that does not apply to them.
Cite the cited study result as context only: HubSpot research referenced in the source found segmented lists produced a 791% increase in email ROI.
caveats: The 791% ROI lift is a third-party study result cited by the source, not a promise for your list.
Every extra opt-in field costs signups, so weigh the segmentation gain against form friction.

cards.title: Make CTR the primary email metric, not open rate
cards.summary: Track clicked actions over opens because Apple privacy changes make open data unreliable and CTR is what predicts revenue.
cards.use_when: Choosing the KPI for a store email program and reviewing send-to-send performance.
steps: Decide on the definition first: CTR can mean clicks as a share of all recipients, or of those who opened — the two produce very different numbers.
Use clicks-as-share-of-sent as the metric tied to action, since it is independent of open-tracking accuracy.
Report both so you can tell an open-rate problem from a click-rate problem.
Evaluate over a rolling period rather than per email, balancing 'deposit' sends against harder 'withdraw' asks.
Use the source's own figures only as orientation: roughly 35.7% open rate and 8.5% CTR across three months on his list, which he treats as a strong CTR.
Accept that open-rate accuracy is degraded by privacy changes and treat it as directional.
caveats: The 35.7% / 8.5% figures are one sender's list — not a benchmark to hold yourself to.
The source states he is confident in CTR but not in the open-rate reporting.

cards.title: Split-test subject lines on a slice, then send the winner
cards.summary: Test subject lines (and preview text) on a small portion of the list, then blast the winning variant to the rest.
cards.use_when: Optimizing subject-line performance for recurring brand emails or product campaigns.
steps: Create two variants of the subject line and let the platform send each to a small percentage of the list.
Wait for the winner to emerge, then send that variant to the remainder.
Model the same pattern used for video thumbnails: automated variant testing picks the better performer.
Weigh brand consistency: if you are building a named recurring format, keeping the same prefix every time can cost some short-term open rate in exchange for a habit-driven long-term open.
Optimize the preview text as a separate asset — it is the first roughly 150 characters shown and the source reports up to a 24% open-rate lift from crafting it (source-reported figure).
Do not let the preview default to the first 150 characters of the body, which is often a greeting and carries no curiosity value.
caveats: The 24% preview-text lift is attributed to the source's reported experience, not a guaranteed result.
Fixing a branded subject prefix sacrifices subject-line testing upside; the source frames this as a deliberate trade-off.

cards.title: Send at the right day and hour for B2C vs B2B
cards.summary: Match send day and time window to audience type, since consumer and business inboxes peak differently.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a store's campaign or newsletter sends across a week.
steps: For B2C, prefer Monday and Tuesday based on Nielsen/Neil Patel data cited in the source, with about an 18% average open-rate increase.
For B2B, prefer Wednesday (source notes Wednesday delivered a comparable lift to the B2C Monday/Tuesday effect).
Justify it as attention availability: consumers are more distracted early week; business buyers catch their breath midweek.
Send in the pre-lunch and post-lunch windows — roughly 10:00–noon and 1:00–3:00 — since the first thing in the morning is dominated by genuine business mail.
If you operate in a single time zone, use these windows deliberately; if your list is spread internationally, do not over-invest in timing precision.
Pick a reference time zone and stay consistent with it.
caveats: These day/time effects are described as small lifts, not transformative — the source calls them 'golden BBs'.
Relevance drops sharply for multi-time-zone audiences.

cards.title: Keep cadence high but content value-only
cards.summary: Send roughly three times a week if every send is genuinely valuable, and fold the CTA into the value rather than running separate promo emails.
cards.use_when: Setting the sending frequency and give/ask balance for a store's list.
steps: Start at once a month if you are not mailing, then increase as quality holds.
Target about three sends a week only when content stays strictly value-driven; the source reports this as the sweet spot after talking to experienced email marketers.
Skip the classic promo/educational rotation: make every email valuable and simply make the path to your offer easily available, the way a link-in-bio works.
Remove the need to balance a give/ask ratio by never treating a send as pure ask.
Note the alternative: the source personally dislikes committing to a cadence and prefers sending when he has good material.
If frequency is harming quality, lower frequency rather than lower quality.
caveats: 'Three times a week' is passed on as advice from other email marketers, explicitly labelled as not a rule.
Emailing more often than a store can produce honest value is expected to burn the list.

cards.title: Optimize for mobile rendering before sending
cards.summary: Check how every email renders on mobile, since most recipients will read it there and poor rendering kills clicks.
cards.use_when: Final QA before sending any store email, especially image- or layout-heavy templates.
steps: Preview the email in both desktop and mobile formats before sending.
Fix layout breakage now, because images and multi-column blocks are the most likely to mangle on small screens.
Weigh the mobile share: the source cites roughly 58–60% of global internet traffic on mobile devices.
Treat broken rendering as a direct CTR problem — the source says unprofessional-looking mobile layouts plummet click-through rates, with e-commerce most at risk because of heavy imagery.
Consider that plain-text, image-free email sidesteps most mobile rendering risk entirely (see the plain-text card).
caveats: The 58–60% mobile traffic figure is global internet traffic, not email opens specifically.
Mobile preview tools vary by client and interface — verify in your current email platform.

cards.title: Confine links and CTAs to one per objective
cards.summary: Use one or two links per email, each tied to a distinct audience or objective, instead of sprinkling many links.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many links and buttons a store email should contain.
steps: Raise the link count deliberately: the source disagrees with the common 'one link only' rule and says one or two is safe.
Require a clear reason for a reader to pick one link over another — each link should serve a different objective or audience.
Avoid five or more links, which the source calls aggressive.
Put a genuinely interesting nugget in the email and send readers to the full asset rather than pasting the whole blog post into the email.
Treat clicks as training: each rewarded click makes the next click more likely, so build the habit deliberately over time.
Keep the CTA contextual — the bridge into the link should follow from the email's specific content, not from a stock button pasted into every send.
caveats: Click training only works if the destination is good; a weak linked asset degrades future click behavior.
The one-link rule is a real practice elsewhere — this is presented as a situational alternative, not an absolute.

cards.title: Use annual renewal fees to lift revenue without touching the headline price
cards.summary: Add a one-time annual fee on top of a monthly subscription, charged after the first year, to increase revenue without hurting front-end conversion.
cards.use_when: Pricing a subscription, membership or replenishment program in a store.
steps: Set the annual fee at about one to three months of the monthly price.
Charge it only after the subscriber has stayed a year, so it never appears in the advertised entry price that drives signups.
Reason about timing: someone who has already stayed twelve months is unlikely to leave over it.
Estimate the impact: the source states the fee adds roughly 8–24% to revenue at no added cost, and on a 20% margin business that can roughly double profit.
Example from the source: a $39/month plan with a $99 annual renewal moves annual revenue per customer from $468 to $567, a 21% increase and an effective $47/month.
Keep advertised pricing unchanged because advertised price drives conversion.
caveats: All figures are the source's illustrative math, not tested results across businesses.
This works for recurring/recurring-charge models; it does not transfer to one-off product sales.
Disclose the fee clearly in terms of service to avoid chargeback and trust damage.

cards.title: Turn testimonials into hooks by asking for the worst moment
cards.summary: Collect testimonial answers as a specific worst-moment story rather than a before/after narrative, so the quote works as an ad hook.
cards.use_when: Sourcing customer testimonials for a store's PDP, ads or email content.
steps: Stop asking customers how life was before your product — that produces long stories with no usable hook.
Instead ask one question: what was the worst moment?
Expect a moment, not a summary; the specificity is what makes the hook powerful.

Compare the source's own examples: 'two months away from shutting our doors', 'barely making enough to survive', and two separate testimonials that ended the month with $0 of profit — the detail, not the general struggle, is the value.
Analyze which hooks win by reviewing many testimonials together (the source reviewed 2,500 and found the best shared a pain-based hook).
Deploy the resulting line as the opening of an ad, the first line of an email, or the top of a review block.
caveats: The 2,500-review finding is from Gym Launch testimonials in a coaching context; the transfer to a store's reviews is an adaptation.
Pain-based hooks suit acquisition creative; testimonials used as reassurance on a PDP may need a different, outcome-focused framing.

cards.title: Give away a peeled-off bonus to make list membership worth something
cards.summary: Create exclusive assets that only list subscribers receive, so opt-in is sold on ongoing membership rather than the lead magnet alone.
cards.use_when: Designing the incentive stack for a store's email opt-in.
steps: Identify work you already produced that is valuable but does not fit its main container — the source describes writing book chapters that did not flow with the book.
Finish that material to full quality and reserve it as a subscriber-only gift.
Make it platform-specific so there is a reason to be on the email list specifically, not just somewhere.
Separate the recruitment message: sell regular communication first, then mention the free asset by the way.
Back it with anticipation — tell subscribers a larger announcement is coming and they will hear it first.
Verify the asset is genuinely good before gating it, because unsubscribing after a disappointing reward is the outcome the source says he worries about most.
caveats: A weak lead magnet followed by nothing of ongoing value causes immediate unsubscribes or permanent dormancy.
Exclusive-asset creation requires genuinely spare finished work; manufacturing filler defeats the purpose.

cards.title: Prioritize fast follow-up over almost everything else
cards.summary: Respond to an opt-in within seconds — the source says it could quadruple sales and argues it should be the first operational priority.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to fix first in a store's lead handling and conversion process.
steps: Set up a system that calls or reaches a lead within about 60 seconds of opting in.
Cite the source's basis: an HBR study he refers to showed an average 391% increase in sales, which he translates as roughly quadrupling.
Run the prioritization test: if nothing else on the roadmap can quadruple sales, this should be the first priority.
Reframe staffing as self-funding: the source argues you can afford the coverage out of the sales lift it produces.
Treat it as simple to understand and hard to operate — the constraint is coverage and process, not the idea.
caveats: The 391% is a study figure cited by the source, not a guaranteed outcome for your store.
This applies to businesses with a sales follow-up step — direct-to-consumer self-serve checkouts may have no equivalent action.

cards.title: Focus effort on CTR over open rate over time
cards.summary: Optimize the rolling click-through rate rather than individual sends, treating high-value hard asks as withdrawals against softer sends.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's monthly email mix and reviewing whether the program is trending up or down.
steps: Decide deliberately which sends are deposits (pure value, low ask) and which are withdrawals (a real conversion push).
Avoid asking for the click with equal pressure in every send, since that erodes response over time.
Deliver hidden high-value content behind links — the source cites Google Drive links to video sales letters and other gated assets as an effective pattern — to keep clicks rewarding.
Watch the rolling metric rather than the single send; the source evaluates CTR across a period, not per email.
Note the source's own orientation numbers as context only: about 8.5% CTR, which he interprets as roughly 8,500 clicks per 100,000 sends.
Expect that training the audience to click is what governs future deliverability, since providers read engagement as quality.
caveats: Google Drive link tactics are described by the source as a 2011-era advanced tactic — test whether it still behaves that way in current inbox environments.
The 8.5% CTR is one sender's list, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Use native-style links for deliverability
cards.summary: Route clicks to links that inbox providers already recognize as legitimate rather than to raw hosted sales pages.
cards.use_when: Choosing where a store's email link should point — sales page, video or gated document.
steps: Prefer links to mainstream properties the provider understands, such as a video platform link.
For a sales letter or video sales letter, host the asset where the provider can identify the file type rather than on an unfamiliar domain.
Test rough, duct-taped-looking assets too — the source says they sometimes convert better than polished destinations.
Label this as a 2011-era tactic and verify current behavior before relying on it.
Pair it with the broader principle: align with the provider's objective of delivering high-quality mail rather than looking for hacks.
caveats: The source explicitly flags this as an old tactic, and provider routing behavior changes — verify before depending on it.
Hosting sensitive assets on third-party storage may not suit branded or gated commercial offers.

Covers the strategy of high-value, text-only emails, optimal sending frequency, subject line split testing, and maximizing click-through rates (CTR) over open rates. Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a high-leverage, text-heavy email marketing strategy designed to bypass the Gmail "Promotions" tab, build long-term reader habits, and generate massive ROI by prioritizing short, actionable content over traditional graphic-heavy sales emails. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, newsletter strategy, deliverability, click-through rate, A/B testing, copywriting, B2B email, B2C email] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the ROI of email / explaining how email marketing generates a 35-45x return on investment because the lead acquisition cost is already paid, making it the highest-leverage retention and conversion tool available; deliverability and the promotions tab / detailing the 2011-era tactic of using plain-text formatting, minimal links, and avoiding "money" words to ensure emails land in the primary inbox rather than the Gmail promotions tab (noting that 16.9% of B2B marketing emails fail to reach the inbox entirely); the "Mosie Money Minute" format / breaking down Hormozi's specific email structure: an immediate quote/reward at the top, a single 200-word tactical nugget, a contextual Call to Action (CTA), and a P.S. statement that rewards the reader for finishing; maximizing Click-Through Rate (CTR) / shifting focus from open rates (which are increasingly inaccurate due to Apple Privacy changes) to CTR, emphasizing that training the audience to click by offering high-value hidden content (e.g., Google Drive links to VSLs) is critical for algorithm health; opt-in and engagement loops / utilizing the "Reply Yes" strategy during the lead magnet opt-in process to force engagement, which signals to email servers that the sender is highly reputable; email sending cadence / confirming that a frequency of roughly 3x per week is the sweet spot for maximizing conversions without burning out the list, provided the content remains strictly value-driven; A/B testing subject lines / using split testing to determine the winning subject line on a small percentage of the list before blasting the remainder, while also optimizing the first 150 characters (the preview text) to spike open rates by up to 24%; optimal send times / highlighting data that B2C emails perform best on Mondays and Tuesdays, B2B emails peak on Wednesdays, and the ideal send windows generally fall between 10:00 AM–Noon and 1:00 PM–3:00 PM.

Look for.

The "Reply Yes" Deliverability Hack: The onboarding strategy of requiring new subscribers to physically reply "Yes" to the welcome email to receive their lead magnet, instantly signaling to email providers (like Gmail) that the sender is a trusted contact and bypassing the Promotions tab.

The Plain-Text Paradigm: The deliberate choice to format marketing emails exactly like a message from a friend—heavy text, zero images, and minimal links—to avoid triggering AI spam filters that penalize graphic-heavy "Vegas Strip" style e-commerce templates.

Preview Text Optimization: The tactical focus on meticulously crafting the preview text (the first 150 characters visible before opening) rather than letting it default to generic greetings, which is proven to lift open rates by up to 24%.

The "Contextual CTA" Rule: The principle that Call to Actions must naturally bridge from the specific educational content of the email, rather than using generic, copy-pasted buttons that train readers to ignore them.

Skip. Plugs for the acquisition.com scaling workshops, the School community, and personal anecdotes about Hormozi's hesitation to start an email list.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (standard email formatting), 90% growth (advanced deliverability hacks, copywriting structure, and algorithmic engagement loops). Volume. ~450 words.
